_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: League City's camera referendum asks for voters' preferences without binding the council. Pflugerville's proposed AI charter language would create a different kind of obligation.

introduction.text: League City voters are being asked whether police should continue using fixed license plate reader cameras on public roads. The [published question](c1) says at its opening that the result will be a nonbinding statement of voter preference.
That qualification is the central fact. The referendum can record what voters want. Its own wording does not transfer the decision from the council to the ballot.

paragraphs.text: Pflugerville's charter review commission proposed a section on artificial intelligence protections. Its [recommendation](c10) would require the council to adopt safeguards for data and surveillance technologies and require a responsible AI framework.

The council approved an ordinance ordering a charter amendment election. That establishes an election, not adoption of the proposed charter language. This edition's record does not include verification of the final ballot wording.

sections.heading: The camera contract is another decision

paragraphs.text: Pflugerville also scheduled consideration of a Flock camera lease. At the reporting date, that item remained unvoted. A contract decision and a charter amendment may concern the same technology while carrying different legal effects.

League City's next posted council agenda carried no item naming Flock or license plate reader cameras. It did include a general public comment period. An opportunity to speak is not a scheduled camera vote.

The League City result would express a preference under the question as published. Pflugerville's final ballot and election outcome would determine the charter question. Neither should be described as a camera ban already in force.
